title: Reaction Race
intro: A game for 2 players. Wait for the light, then race to press your button first!

wiring_steps.title: Player 1's button
wiring_steps.text: Unplug the USB cable before you change any wires. Plug it back in when you're done. Start with the power rails: a black wire from GND on your board to the blue (−) rail at the bottom of the breadboard, and a red wire from {{VCC}} to the red (+) rail. Press the player 1 button into the middle of the breadboard so it sits across the gap: its legs go in F2, F4, E2 and E4. Add a wire from {{pin:BUTTON_PIN}} to J2, and a black wire from A4 to the blue (−) rail. (The code turns on the pin's pull-up, so no resistor is needed.)

wiring_steps.title: Player 2's button
wiring_steps.text: Press the player 2 button into the middle of the breadboard so it sits across the gap: its legs go in F26, F28, E26 and E28. Add a wire from {{pin:BUTTON2_PIN}} to J26, and a black wire from A28 to the blue (−) rail. (The code turns on the pin's pull-up, so no resistor is needed.)

wiring_steps.title: The green LED
wiring_steps.text: Push the green "go" LED into holes H13 and H14, with the long leg (+) in H14. Put a 220Ω resistor from G13 across the gap to E13. Add a wire from {{pin:LED_GREEN}} to J14, and a black wire from A13 to the blue (−) rail at the bottom.

wiring_steps.title: The buzzer
wiring_steps.text: The buzzer sits beside the breadboard. Connect its + leg (the red wire, or the leg marked +) to {{pin:BUZZER_PIN}}, and its − leg (the black wire) to the blue (−) rail.

wiring_steps.title: The player LEDs
wiring_steps.text: Each player gets a light. Red is player 1's: Push the red LED into holes H7 and H8, with the long leg (+) in H8. Put a 220Ω resistor from G7 across the gap to E7. Add a wire from {{pin:LED_RED}} to J8, and a black wire from A7 to the blue (−) rail at the bottom. Yellow is player 2's: Push the yellow LED into holes H21 and H22, with the long leg (+) in H22. Put a 220Ω resistor from G21 across the gap to E21. Add a wire from {{pin:LED_YELLOW}} to J22, and a black wire from A21 to the blue (−) rail at the bottom.

steps.title: Test both buttons
steps.text:
Two players, two buttons. First check both work.

**Your task:** Run, open the **Serial Monitor**, and press each button.
hints: In the simulator, click each button on the breadboard.
Hold a button and you'll see its name over and over.
If nothing shows, check each button's wires.

steps.title: How fast are you?
steps.text:
`millis()` counts milliseconds since the board started, like a stopwatch that never stops. Take the time when the light comes on, and again when the button is pressed: the difference is your reaction time.

**Your task:** fill in the blank to work out the reaction time.
hints: The reaction time is the time now, take away the time the light came on.
The time now is `millis()`. The start time is in `start`.
steps.success: Most people react in about 200 to 300 milliseconds. How fast are you?

steps.title: Race!
steps.text: **Goal:** a two-player race. After a surprise wait, the GO light comes on. The first player to press wins: their light comes on and the Serial Monitor says `Player 1 wins!` or `Player 2 wins!`. Pressing before GO is a false start: print `Too soon!`.
hints: A `while (true)` loop can keep checking both buttons until one is pressed. `return` leaves `loop()` so the next round starts.
A function `winner(player, lightPin)` saves writing the winning code twice.
Check for a false start straight after the wait, before turning the GO light on.
steps.success: Game on! Get a friend and see who's fastest.

outro: Your reaction game times people to the millisecond with **millis()**, picks a **random** wait so nobody can cheat, and decides a winner with **if / else**.
stretch: Keep score over 5 rounds and announce the champion.
Print the winner's reaction time in milliseconds.
Add a third player with another button and LED.
